extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, agents, and inventors drafting AI / machine learning patent claims (USPTO-focused)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for drafting patent claims and disclosures for AI and machine learning inventions to survive subject-matter-eligibility and enablement scrutiny (with USPTO 2024 guidance in mind). Targets claim language, claim structure (training vs. inference), and specification disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate practical and technological application (avoid abstract idea rejections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate how the invention applies the abstract idea in a practical and technological context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent examiners may argue the invention is merely an abstract idea (e.g., mathematical concept, mental process). To overcome this, show how the claimed AI/ML technique is applied to a concrete technological problem or computer technology context rather than being a pure mathematical or mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on technical specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer concrete, application-specific claim language (instead of generic phrasing like 'a method for data analysis using machine learning').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example substitution: use 'a method for predictive maintenance in industrial machinery, comprising training a neural network on historical sensor data to predict equipment failures'. Specificity helps avoid overlap with prior art and clarifies the practical application; tailor claims to the concrete domain and technical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate training and execution (inference) claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft separate independent claims for the training phase and for the execution/inference phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training-phase claims should recite model architecture, training data, loss/objective functions, hyperparameters, etc. Execution/inference claims should recite deployment, prediction, output use, and how outputs are used in a technological context. Where the execution phase lacks independent substance, include training-phase details in passive clauses to support eligibility/enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish multiple ML models clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple models are involved, explicitly distinguish them in claim language so their respective roles are unambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ordinals and clear labels (e.g., 'first training data' / 'second training data', 'first output' / 'second output') and avoid ambiguous references about which model performs which function to prevent claim indefiniteness and enable precise claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize unique technical aspects of the AI implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight technical features that distinguish the AI/ML invention from human thinking or abstract algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples to emphasize: weighting of nodes in an artificial neural network; retraining of an existing ML model; deploying a trained ML model to different computing devices; specific architectures (CNNs, transformers, GANs); training data preparation (augmentation, sampling); pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation. Use these technical details to show technical character and improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish patent eligibility by showing technical improvements and real‑world application
rubrics_metrics.description: AI inventions are more likely to be patent eligible when they solve concrete technical problems, provide measurable improvements, and explain how those improvements are achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims and specification so they (1) identify a concrete technical problem, (2) describe measurable improvements (metrics, accuracy gains, latency reduction, resource savings), (3) explain the mechanism by which the improvement is achieved, and (4) reflect the technical improvement in claim language; ensure there is a real-world application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align claims with USPTO 2024 AI guidance and eligible examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow USPTO 2024 Subject Matter Eligibility Update examples that identify specific AI applications in computer technology as potentially eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precedent/examples in claim drafting: improving accuracy of speech recognition (eligible), anomaly detection methods tied to specific networks (eligible), AI-driven medical treatment selection (may be eligible if claims show practical application). Tie claims to specific computer/technological implementation details to mirror USPTO-identified eligible categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common pitfalls / anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not draft claims that fall into patterns frequently rejected as abstract or non-enabling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claims that simply recite 'using a machine learning model'; math-only claims with no technical use; claims describing only data manipulation; claims that are merely mental processes implemented 'on a computer'; and purely functional claims without enabling structural disclosure. These anti-patterns increase the risk of abstract-idea rejections or indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sufficient disclosure / enablement (35 U.S.C. 112 / Article 83)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must disclose enough detail for enablement and written description, particularly for AI/ML innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose model architecture (if novel), training data type and characteristics, loss/objective functions, hyperparameters or hyperparameter ranges, performance metrics, and sufficient detail to reproduce the technical effect. Ensure functional claim elements are supported by structural/algorithmic disclosure to avoid failing enablement or written description requirements.
